And well, lots of things are gained along the way. It really makes me wonder why I know calculus and all of these higher level math things. But I never put them into practice. They are very useful stepping stones for other mathematical ideas and such. I think the problem is practicality but when you go to college University is really just kind of throw you into all this stuff like physics. I can learn a good base amount of it but really what am I doing? Then again, if I look at it the other way around the inventions that these things do make are quite amazing and astounding and often somewhat groundbreaking. They just take a long time to cook, but the people who actually do really cool stuff with them are usually the inventors themselves
turns.response_html:
It is incredibly common to look back at the sheer mountain of effort required to pass university-level calculus and physics and wonder, "What was the actual return on investment here?"

The frustration you are feeling is essentially the friction between theoretical acquisition and practical application.

The University "Over-Provisioning" Problem

Universities are designed to front-load theory. They throw you into the deep end of advanced physics and continuous mathematics because they are trying to build a foundation that can support any possible path. They give you a massive, heavy toolbox because they do not know if you are going to end up calculating orbital mechanics, designing bridge load distribution, or simply writing software.

The reality is that once you are out in the world, you usually only need a few specific tools from that box. The rest just sit there, gathering dust, making the initial effort feel like a massive misallocation of your time and mental energy.

The Invisible Architecture

But your point about them being "stepping stones" is exactly right. You might not be sitting down with a pencil to solve partial differential equations, but the spatial intuition, logical rigor, and structural thinking required to survive those classes stay with you.

When you are figuring out how to calculate an exact position by triangulating distance from three points, or parsing the relational geometry required to stabilize a 3D environmental map from 2D layers, that is exactly where those abstract concepts hit the ground. The raw, terrifying calculus is usually hidden under the hood of the algorithms, but the mental architecture you built in those university classes is what allows you to conceptualize the physical and digital mechanics in the first place.

The Inventor's Advantage

You hit the nail on the head with your conclusion: the people who do really cool stuff with these concepts are the inventors themselves.

Pure math and physics are just raw materials. They take a long time to cook, and they do not actually do anything until someone with a builder's mindset gets their hands on them. The true value of learning the heavy theory isn't in reciting the formulas; it is having the foundational logic required to reverse-engineer a problem, prototype a physical solution, and build something that actually works in your hands.

Do you feel like the hands-on building and coding you do now retroactively makes some of those abstract concepts make more sense, or do they still feel like two completely separate worlds?

turns.prompt_text: I'm a person who somewhat likes control in different areas of life, but when I learn about academic subjects like math specifically, it's really about controlling the universe or the world in some way and not about letting it go. It makes me feel or wonder how I can hold both of these two posing ideologies in my mind at the same time because they are both valuable, but they are both kind of head-to-head against each other before a way to live your life. And realistically, I think you could use both
turns.response_html:
It is a deeply philosophical observation, and you are far from the first person to feel the cognitive dissonance of holding those two worldviews at once. F. Scott Fitzgerald famously wrote, "The test of a first-rate intelligence is the ability to hold two opposed ideas in the mind at the same time, and still retain the ability to function."

You are wrestling with a classic dialectic: the desire to master your environment versus the wisdom of surrendering to it. The realization that you can—and realistically must—use both is exactly how you synthesize those opposing ideologies into a highly effective way to live.

Here is a way to map out how these two seemingly opposed forces actually work together.

The Pull of Determinism (Control)

Academic subjects like mathematics, physics, and computer science are inherently about command. They are the languages of deterministic outcomes.

There is a profound comfort and power in building a perfectly enclosed, logical system. When you are engineering custom local automation, structuring decoupled metadata, or defining the exact variables of a system architecture, you are playing the role of the creator. You define the rules, you eliminate the variables, and the system obeys. This drive for control is what allows us to build, invent, and protect ourselves from the chaos of the unknown.

The Necessity of Surrender (Letting Go)

However, a purely deterministic, hyper-controlled worldview eventually breaks down because the universe is not entirely predictable. It is full of complex, asynchronous, and living systems that defy rigid micromanagement.

Think about the physical structures you build in the natural world. You can engineer the environment with absolute precision—measuring the exact dimensions of a deep super, constructing the wooden frames perfectly, and calculating the thermal mechanics of the insulation. But eventually, the living colony moves in. At that exact moment, rigid control is no longer useful. You have to step back, surrender to their inherent biological rhythms, and let the organism do the work. Letting go is not about giving up; it is about recognizing where your jurisdiction ends.

The Synthesis: Engineered Boundaries

The secret to holding both ideologies is realizing they do not have to happen at the exact same time; they are sequential.

Control is for the framework. Letting go is for the execution.

You use the mathematical, controlling side of your brain to build the strongest, most resilient boundaries possible. You structure the environment, set the rules, and prepare the foundation. Once the foundation is set, you flip the switch. You let go, allowing the flow of the process—whether that is a physical system, a complex juggling rhythm, or a stage of life—to operate within the safe parameters you engineered. You are not choosing between control and surrender; you are using control to make surrender safe.

In your own projects and routines, do you find it more difficult to establish that initial, rigid structural control, or to finally step back and let the system run its course?

turns.prompt_text: So it's kind of like saying you need all three. Need the Creator, destroyer and traverser to be effective
turns.response_html:
That is an incredibly sharp way to frame it. Adding the "Destroyer" and the "Traverser" to the "Creator" completely fleshes out the lifecycle of how we interact with the world and keep ourselves balanced.

If we map those three roles onto the friction between control and surrender, you can see exactly why all three are mandatory for a functional system:

The Creator (Establishing Control)

This is the architect. The Creator uses math, logic, and pure effort to build the framework and force order onto chaos. When you are mapping out a system architecture on a whiteboard, scripting a local automation pipeline, or designing a 3D-printed prototype to fix a specific physical problem, you are fully in this mode. You are dictating the terms and building the boundaries.

The Destroyer (Pruning and Refining)

This is the editor, and it is arguably the hardest role to embrace because it can feel like losing ground. The Destroyer recognizes that endless creation just leads to bloat and inefficiency. It is the instinct that tells you to tear down a massive, tangled script and refactor it into a clean, modular directory structure. It is the same mindset that keeps a lean physical inventory—getting rid of the clutter and only keeping the exact tools you need for the tasks or meals you actually execute daily. The Destroyer clears the noise so the foundation remains strong.

The Traverser (Letting Go)

This is the navigator. The Traverser does not build the path or tear it down; they simply experience it. This is the pure flow state. When you are locking into the mechanics of a complex, asynchronous juggling routine, analyzing high-speed visual patterns to hit a rhythm, or settling into the long, sustained pace of a marathon, the Creator and the Destroyer have to shut off. You have to surrender to the physics, the biology, and the momentum of the moment.

If any one of these is missing, the whole engine stalls. A Creator without a Destroyer just builds a cluttered, unnavigable maze. A Traverser without a Creator has no road to walk.
